payload.text: The Lambertian model approximates diffuse reflection with a simple BRDF where outgoing intensity depends on surface orientation and reflectance.
The Lambertian model simplifies complex surface reflectance by assuming purely diffuse reflection, making it easier to analyze and simulate light reflection.

In general, BRDFs can be quite complicated (see @Matusik2002), describing both diffuse and specular components of reflection. Even surfaces with completely diffuse reflections can give complicated reflectance distributions @Oren1994. A useful approximation describing diffuse reflection is the Lambertian model, with a particularly simple BRDF, which we denote as $F_L$. The outgoing ray intensity, $\ell_{\texttt{out}}$, is a function only of the surface orientation relative to the incoming and outgoing ray directions, the wavelength, a scalar surface reflectance, and the incoming light power:
$$
\ell_{\texttt{out}} = F_{L} \left( \ell_{\texttt{in}} (\lambda), \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{p} \right)  = a \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda) \left( \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p} \right),
$$ {#eq-lambert}

where $a$ is the surface reflectance, or albedo, $\mathbf{n}$ is the surface normal vector, and $\mathbf{p}$ points toward the source of the incident light. Note that the brightness of the outgoing light ray depends on the orientation of the surface relative to the incident ray, as well as the reflectance, $a$, of the surface. For a Lambertian surface, the intensity of the reflected light is a function of the direction of the incoming light ray, but not a function of the outgoing direction of the ray, $\mathbf{q}$.

payload.prompt: What property distinguishes a Lambertian surface from a glossy one?
choices: Lambertian surfaces reflect more total light
Lambertian surfaces look equally bright from every viewing direction
Lambertian surfaces don't reflect any light at all
Lambertian surfaces only reflect red light
payload.explanation_correct: Right — a Lambertian (perfectly diffuse) surface has constant radiance regardless of viewing angle. Matte paper is a good real-world approximation.
payload.explanation_wrong: Lambertian surfaces are *view-independent*: radiance is constant across viewing directions. Glossy surfaces aren't.

payload.text: Imagine walking around a matte chalk sphere vs. a polished metal sphere. Which one keeps the same apparent brightness from every angle?
